result.summary: Hercules begins his labours for Eurystheus. He kills the Nemean lion and the Lernaean hydra, captures the Cerynitian hind and Erymanthian boar, cleans the stables of Augeas, drives off the Stymphalian birds, and brings back the Cretan bull and the mares of Diomedes.

scenes.title: The Nemean lion
scenes.summary: Hercules kills the invulnerable lion at Nemea by strangling it, and Eurystheus, terrified, bans him from the city.
scenes.stakes: Hercules risks death against an invulnerable beast, and Molorchus will sacrifice to him as a dead hero if he fails.

scenes.title: The Lernaean hydra
scenes.summary: With Iolaus's help Hercules defeats the many-headed hydra and poisons his arrows with its gall. Eurystheus refuses to count the labour.
scenes.stakes: Hercules is held fast by the hydra and its regrowing heads, and the labour may not count.

scenes.title: The Cerynitian hind
scenes.summary: Hercules hunts the golden-horned hind for a year and appeases Artemis, who is angry at him.
scenes.stakes: The anger of Artemis and Apollo at the harm to the sacred animal.

scenes.title: Pholus, the centaurs and the boar
scenes.summary: Hercules is entertained by Pholus, and opening the wine brings a centaur fight in which Chiron and Pholus die. He then captures the boar.
scenes.stakes: Hercules is attacked by armed centaurs, and his friends Pholus and Chiron are accidentally wounded.

scenes.title: The stables of Augeas
scenes.summary: Hercules cleans the cattle-yard by diverting rivers, but Augeas cheats him. Hercules rescues Dexamenus's daughter from Eurytion, and Eurystheus rejects the labour.
scenes.stakes: Hercules's promised tithe of cattle, and the labour's validity.

scenes.title: The Stymphalian birds
scenes.summary: With castanets from Athena, Hercules frightens the birds from their wood and shoots them.
scenes.stakes: Hercules cannot drive the birds out without help.

scenes.title: The Cretan bull
scenes.summary: Hercules catches the bull in Crete and shows it to Eurystheus before releasing it, after which it ravages Greece.
scenes.stakes: Hercules must capture a savage bull.

scenes.title: The mares of Diomedes
scenes.summary: Hercules takes the man-eating mares, loses Abderus, kills Diomedes and founds Abdera.
scenes.stakes: Hercules faces the armed Bistones, and Abderus is killed by the mares.

analysis.text: The labours show strength tested by cunning and endurance, and Eurystheus's refusals to count some labours make the penance harder.
Many episodes explain local cults, place names and foundations such as Abdera, tying the hero to sites across Greece.

legacy.text: The Nemean lion's skin and the hydra became lasting symbols in art, and 'Herculean task' and 'Augean stables' entered English.
Disney's Hercules (1997) features the hydra, while the Nemean lion appears in the Percy Jackson series.

fun_facts.text: The Library is attributed to Apollodorus but probably dates from the first or second century AD.

language_notes.text: "That" refers to the Delphic oracle's command, given just before this passage, that Hercules serve Eurystheus for twelve years and perform the labours set him.
"Sacrifice to him as to a hero" means offering the funeral-style rites given to the honoured dead, not the rites for a god.
"Day-laborer" means a poor man hired for daily wages; Molorchus is humble, yet hosts Hercules.
"Built up the one entrance" means he blocked it with stones or similar material.
"Manhood" here means manly courage and strength.
"Purified" refers to ritual cleansing of the guilt of a killing, which a killer needed before being received again.
"Gall" is bile, here made venomous by the hydra's poison.
Labour: one of the twelve tasks imposed on Hercules by Eurystheus, king of Mycenae, as penance.
"Howbeit" is archaic for "however" or "nevertheless", marking a contrast with the previous sentence.
The jar of wine was a communal gift to the centaurs, so opening it without their consent was a breach of their shared property.
Brands are burning pieces of wood taken from a fire, used here as missiles.
Prometheus, the Titan punished by Zeus for giving fire to humans, here gives up his own immortality in exchange for Chiron's death.
"Tithe" literally means a tenth part; here Hercules asks for a tenth of Augeas's cattle as payment.
"Accosted" means approached and spoke to him directly.
"Pack out of" is a colloquial way of saying "leave at once"; it conveys Augeas's angry dismissal.
"Betrothing perforce" means promising his daughter in marriage under compulsion, since Eurytion was forcing the match.
"Embosomed" is archaic for enclosed or nestled within, as if cradled by the wood.
"Brazen" means made of brass or bronze; castanets are clappers that make a sharp, loud rattling noise.
"Enjoined on him" means commanded or imposed on him as a task, here by Eurystheus.
Zeus, in the form of a bull, carried the Phoenician princess Europa across the sea to Crete. Acusilaus is an early Greek mythographer.
Minos had vowed to sacrifice whatever emerged from the sea, but kept the beautiful bull and offered a lesser one, which angered Poseidon.
"Minion" here means a favourite or beloved companion, in the sense of a young male lover.
"Done to death" is an archaic phrase meaning killed.
"As it is called" signals the author's caution about the name Olympus, which also belonged to the famous mountain of the gods.

context_notes.text: Typhon was a monstrous giant of Greek myth, father of many monsters, including the Nemean lion in this version.
Zeus appears here though the translator usually writes Jove; this translation uses Zeus in this text. Saviour Zeus was invoked for deliverance from danger.
Lerna was a marshy district near Argos, known in myth as the hydra's haunt.
Iolaus was Hercules' nephew and charioteer, and his regular companion in the labours.
Eurystheus later also rejects the cleaning of the Augean stables, so the twelve labours become more than twelve in count.
Artemis was the goddess of hunting and wild animals, so harming her sacred hind would offend her.
Centaurs were creatures part man and part horse, usually wild and violent. Pholus was an exception, being hospitable.
Chiron was a wise, kindly centaur who taught heroes such as Achilles. He differed from the other centaurs.
Poseidon was the god of the sea. Eleusis was a town in Attica, later famous for its mysteries.
Elis was a region in the western Peloponnese. Augeas's wealth in cattle drives the story of this labour.
Eurystheus disqualified labours on technicalities. Hercules was meant to complete ten, which became twelve once this and the Hydra labour were rejected.
Athena often aids Hercules. Hephaestus was the divine smith, so a bronze instrument from him fits.
Minos was the legendary king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa.
The bull later became the Marathonian bull, which Theseus eventually captured.
The Bistones were a Thracian people, and Thrace was regarded by Greeks as a wild northern land.

literary_notes.text: Eurystheus hiding in a jar and communicating through a herald paints him as a cowardly, petty king, contrasting with Hercules.
The immortal central head suggests a threat that cannot be wholly destroyed, which is why it must be buried under a rock.
Hercules' strength makes the problem worse: every blow meant to destroy produces more heads.
Eurystheus dismisses the victory on a technicality, though he never faced any danger himself.
Pholus's raw meat and Hercules's roast meat contrast the centaur's wild nature with the hero's civilized habits.
Chiron, the immortal healer, suffers a wound he cannot heal and cannot escape through death, so his immortality becomes a torment.
Pholus marvels at the arrow's smallness and is then killed by it, an ironic reversal of his own words.
Augeas calls on arbitration to deny a bargain he made, while the cleaning itself, cheaply done, was plainly accomplished; his bad faith costs him his son's loyalty.
Hercules succeeds by ingenuity as well as strength, using a divine gift to scare the birds out of hiding before shooting them.
Minos's attempt to cheat the god by keeping the bull makes the animal savage, so his greed brings about the harm.
Abderus, left to guard the mares, is killed by them, so the chosen guardian becomes their victim.
